0

Where the ground shifts under you

Everything you have done so far was partial equilibrium: one consumer, one market, prices taken as given (exogenously set). You maximized $u(x,y)$ subject to $p_x x + p_y y = m$ and moved on.

General equilibrium asks a harder question. There is no outside. There are only people, and whatever they already own. Nobody hands anyone income — your income is the market value of your own stuff. Nobody hands anyone a price — prices have to come out of the model, adjusting until the amount people want to buy equals the amount people want to sell.

The one-sentence version. In partial equilibrium, $m$ is a given and $p$ is a given. In general equilibrium, $m = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y$ is endogenous and $p$ is endogenous. That single change is the whole unit.

1

The setup, once, for the whole sheet

Two people, A and B. Two goods, $x$ and $y$. No production — the goods already exist and are already owned. All anyone can do is trade.

SymbolNameWhat it means here
$\omega_A = (\omega_{Ax}, \omega_{Ay})$A's endowmentWhat A walks in owning. Not a choice.
$\omega_B = (\omega_{Bx}, \omega_{By})$B's endowmentWhat B walks in owning.
$(x_A, y_A),\ (x_B, y_B)$an allocationWho ends up with what after trading.
$X = \omega_{Ax} + \omega_{Bx}$total endowment of $x$Fixed. Trade moves it around; it never grows.
$Y = \omega_{Ay} + \omega_{By}$total endowment of $y$Same.
$p = p_x/p_y$the price ratioThe only price that matters. See the note below.
$u_i(x_i, y_i)$$i$'s utility functionTheir tastes. Mostly Cobb–Douglas $x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$ on this sheet.
$m_i = p\,\omega_{ix} + \omega_{iy}$$i$'s incomeThe market value of what they own. Endogenous — it moves with $p$.
$\mathrm{MRS}_i$marginal rate of substitutionHow many units of $y$ person $i$ would give up for one more unit of $x$. For $x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$: $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\cdot\frac{y}{x}$.

Feasibility. An allocation is feasible when nothing is invented and nothing is destroyed:

$$x_A + x_B = X \qquad\text{and}\qquad y_A + y_B = Y$$

Only the ratio is real. If you double both prices, every budget constraint is unchanged and every choice is unchanged. So prices are only pinned down relative to each other. The standard move is to normalize: set $p_y = 1$ and write $p_x = p$. Then "$p$" always means "units of $y$ per unit of $x$." Choosing which good is the numeraire never changes the real answer — only the labels.

The running example (memorize these six numbers)

Almost every worked step on this sheet uses the same economy, so you can watch one story develop instead of learning six:

$$u_A(x_A,y_A) = x_A^{3/4} y_A^{1/4}, \qquad \omega_A = (4, 8)$$ $$u_B(x_B,y_B) = x_B^{1/4} y_B^{3/4}, \qquad \omega_B = (8, 4)$$ $$X = 12, \qquad Y = 12$$

Read the tension out loud before doing any algebra: A puts three-quarters of her weight on $x$ but owns only 4 units of it. B puts three-quarters of his weight on $y$ but owns only 4 units of it. Each person is stuck holding a pile of the thing the other one wants. Everything that follows is just the market working that out.

And here is the finished picture, up front. Everything this sheet builds lives in one diagram with just six pieces. Do not try to absorb it now — each piece gets its own tab. Just notice how few parts there are, and come back to this picture whenever you lose the thread: every tab is adding exactly one labeled piece to it.

2

Two questions, and never confuse them

Question 1 — efficiency

Which allocations waste nothing?

This question has no prices in it at all. It is a pure engineering question about tastes and quantities. The answer is the set of Pareto optimal allocations, which trace out the contract curve.

Tool: $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$.

Tabs 1–3.

Question 2 — equilibrium

Which allocation does a market actually deliver?

Now prices are central. Each person takes $p$ as given, maximizes from their own endowment, and we hunt for the $p$ that makes the two shopping lists add up to what exists.

Tool: $\mathrm{MRS}_i = p$ for each $i$, plus market clearing.

Tabs 4–5.

The punchline of the unit is that these two questions have a shocking amount to do with each other. That relationship is the two Welfare Theorems (tab 6), and it is the single most exam-worthy idea in this block of the course.

The solve procedure lives in its own tab. ⚙ The Algorithm lays out the seven-step recipe for finding a competitive equilibrium, with the running example above worked next to every step. Skim it now so you know it exists; it will make full sense by tab 5.

3

How to use this sheet

Tabs 1–2 build the picture and answer the efficiency question. Drag things around in the Box Explorer until the tangency condition feels obvious rather than memorized.

Tab 3 runs the same box through all four preference types you know — Cobb–Douglas, complements, substitutes, quasilinear — because the exam will not always hand you a smooth interior tangency.

Tabs 4–5 put prices in and solve for equilibrium two ways: by algebra, and by offer curves.

Tab 6 is the theory payoff. Practice is nine problems in scaffolded parts. Cheat Sheet is what to reread the morning of the test.

The Sandbox: play first, vocabulary later

Before a single definition, here is the entire model in your hands. Two people, A and B, are splitting 12 units of good $x$ and 12 units of good $y$ between them. The gold dot is one particular split — drag it anywhere.

The green curve collects every split that A likes exactly as much as the current one; the copper curve does the same for B (B reads the box upside-down, from the top-right corner). The shaded region between them is every alternative split that would make both people happier at once.

Why does a gold region mean both people can win?

Because wherever it exists, the two people disagree about what a unit of $x$ is worth. Look at the MRS readouts at the starting split (MRS — the marginal rate of substitution — is just each person's going rate: how many $y$'s they would trade for one more $x$): A would happily give up 6 units of $y$ for one more $x$, while B would part with an $x$ for anything more than $\tfrac16$ of a $y$. When one person values something at 6 and the other at $\tfrac16$, any swap at a rate in between — say one $x$ for one $y$ — leaves both sides feeling they got the better end of the deal. The gold region is just that disagreement drawn as an area: every point inside it is a version of "trade $x$ toward A and $y$ toward B at some in-between rate."

And that is also why trading eventually stops. Each swap nudges the two valuations toward each other — A, gaining $x$, values the next one a little less; B, losing $x$, values it a little more. The gold region shrinks as they converge, and the moment the two MRS readouts agree, it vanishes: there is no in-between rate left, no deal both would sign. Getting rid of the lens is not a loss — it means every mutually beneficial trade has already been made.

Three things to discover before reading anything else

1. Drag the dot around and watch the shaded region. Wherever it exists, the current split is leaving happiness on the table — there are other splits both people would prefer.

2. Hunt for spots where the shaded region vanishes. When you find one, the two curves just touch instead of crossing. At such a point, nobody can be made happier without hurting the other.

3. Now notice there are many such spots — turn on the curve toggle and drag along it. An entire curve of them, running corner to corner.

You have just discovered every big idea of this unit. The shaded region is called the lens, the untouchable spots are Pareto optimal allocations, and the curve through all of them is the contract curve. Tab 1 (The Box) now walks through this same picture formally — go there next, and everything will already feel familiar.

The two master algorithms, with the running example beside them

Every question in this unit is one of exactly two kinds, and the very first thing to do with any problem is decide which kind it is:

The question mentions prices, markets, trading, or equilibrium — "find the competitive equilibrium," "what price clears the market?"

→ Algorithm 1 below: solve the market-clearing problem.

The question never mentions prices — "find the Pareto optimal allocations," "derive the contract curve," "is this allocation efficient?"

→ Algorithm 2 below: solve the efficiency problem. No prices anywhere in it.

Both algorithms are laid out the same way: the left column is the general form — what you write on any problem — and the right column executes each step on the running example from Start Here, the one worth memorizing:

$$u_A = x_A^{3/4}y_A^{1/4},\ \ \omega_A = (4,8) \qquad u_B = x_B^{1/4}y_B^{3/4},\ \ \omega_B = (8,4) \qquad X = Y = 12$$

Cover the right column with your hand, run the left column yourself, then uncover and compare line by line.

1

Algorithm 1 — competitive equilibrium (market clearing)

The step, in general
Executed on the running example

Step 0Identify the preference type.

Cobb–Douglas, complements, substitutes, or quasilinear? This decides which demand rule you use in step 3 and whether to expect an interior tangency or a corner. Ten seconds here saves a page of wrong algebra. (tab 3)

Both utilities are $x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$ — Cobb–Douglas, with exponents $(\alpha_A, \beta_A) = \left(\tfrac34, \tfrac14\right)$ for A and $(\alpha_B, \beta_B) = \left(\tfrac14, \tfrac34\right)$ for B.

So: the share rule will give demands, and the equilibrium will be a smooth interior tangency — no corners to worry about.

Step 1Normalize.

Only the price ratio matters, so set $p_y = 1$ and $p_x = p$. One unknown price, not two.

$p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$.

From here on, "$p$" means units of $y$ per unit of $x$.

Step 2Write each income as endowment value.

$$m_i = p\,\omega_{ix} + \omega_{iy}$$

Income is endogenous — it moves when $p$ moves. This is the step that makes it general equilibrium; never plug in a fixed number for $m$. (tab 4)

$$m_A = 4p + 8 \qquad m_B = 8p + 4$$

Note the symmetry: A's income rises faster in $p$ than B's falls behind — A owns less $x$, so a higher $p$ helps B more. That tension is what the market will resolve.

Step 3Get each demand as a function of $p$.

Apply the demand rule from step 0 with the income from step 2. For Cobb–Douglas, the share rule:

$$x_i = \frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_i+\beta_i}\cdot\frac{m_i}{p}, \qquad y_i = \frac{\beta_i}{\alpha_i+\beta_i}\,m_i$$

When the exponents sum to 1 (as here), the share is just the exponent itself.

(tab 4; other types: complements → $\frac{m}{p+1}$, substitutes → corner comparison, quasilinear → $\mathrm{MRS}=p$)

$$x_A = \frac34\cdot\frac{4p+8}{p} = 3 + \frac6p$$

$$x_B = \frac14\cdot\frac{8p+4}{p} = 2 + \frac1p$$

(You will not need the $y$ demands until step 5 — Walras' Law is about to make the $y$ market redundant.)

Step 4Clear ONE market.

$$x_A(p) + x_B(p) = X \;\Longrightarrow\; p^*$$

By Walras' Law the $y$ market then clears automatically — solving both is wasted work. (tabs 4–5)

$$3 + \frac6p + 2 + \frac1p = 12$$

$$5 + \frac7p = 12 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac7p = 7 \;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{p^* = 1}$$

Step 5Substitute back.

Plug $p^*$ into all four demand functions. An equilibrium is a price and an allocation — report $p^*$, $(x_A,y_A)$, and $(x_B,y_B)$, always. (tab 5)

$x_A = 3+6 = 9$,   $y_A = \frac14(4+8) = 3$

$x_B = 2+1 = 3$,   $y_B = \frac34(8+4) = 9$

$$\boxed{\ p^* = 1,\quad A = (9,3),\quad B = (3,9)\ }$$

Step 6Run the checks.

(a) The other market clears; (b) each budget balances at $p^*$; (c) both people are at least as well off as at $\omega$; (d) the allocation sits on the contract curve — which it must, by the First Welfare Theorem.

If any check fails, the error is upstream — usually in step 2. (tabs 5–6)

(a) $y$ market: $3 + 9 = 12 = Y$ ✓

(b) A spends $1(9)+3 = 12$; owns $1(4)+8 = 12$ ✓ (B mirrors)

(c) $u_A:\ 4.76 \to 6.84$ and $u_B:\ 4.76 \to 6.84$ ✓

(d) contract curve $y_A = \frac{3x_A}{27-2x_A}$ at $x_A = 9$: $\ \frac{27}{9} = 3$ ✓

2

Algorithm 2 — Pareto optimal allocations (the contract curve)

This one answers the other question: which allocations waste nothing? Notice what is absent from every step below: no $p$, no incomes, no budget lines — and no endowment. Efficiency is a statement about tastes and totals only. (The full derivation with pictures is tab 2 • Pareto & Contract Curve; the interactive version is the ✦ Derivation Lab.)

The step, in general
Executed on the running example

Step 0Identify the preference type.

Same reflex as Algorithm 1, different payoff: smooth and interior (Cobb–Douglas, quasilinear) → the tangency condition applies. Kinked (complements) or linear (substitutes) → the MRS is undefined or never equal, so argue directly from the definition of efficiency instead. (tab 3)

Both Cobb–Douglas — smooth, strictly convex, both goods always wanted.

So the tangency condition $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$ is the right tool, and the efficient set will be a smooth curve through the interior.

Step 1Write A's MRS in A's own coordinates.

For $u = x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$, the shortcut:

$$\mathrm{MRS} = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}\cdot\frac{y}{x}$$

With $\alpha_A = \tfrac34$, $\beta_A = \tfrac14$:

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{3/4}{1/4}\cdot\frac{y_A}{x_A} = 3\,\frac{y_A}{x_A}$$

Step 2Write B's MRS — then translate it into A's coordinates.

Use feasibility to eliminate B's variables:

$$x_B = X - x_A, \qquad y_B = Y - y_A$$

This substitution is the step people skip, and skipping it leaves you with four unknowns and one equation. Everything must be in $x_A$ and $y_A$ before step 3.

With $\alpha_B = \tfrac14$, $\beta_B = \tfrac34$:

$$\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{1/4}{3/4}\cdot\frac{y_B}{x_B} = \frac13\cdot\frac{12 - y_A}{12 - x_A}$$

Step 3Set them equal and clear the fractions.

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$$

Cross-multiply. Do not expect the cross terms to cancel — sometimes they do (identical tastes), usually they combine.

$$3\,\frac{y_A}{x_A} = \frac13\cdot\frac{12-y_A}{12-x_A}$$

$$9\,y_A(12 - x_A) = x_A(12 - y_A)$$

Step 4Solve for $y_A$ as a function of $x_A$.

Expand, collect every $y_A$ term on one side, factor it out, divide. The result is the contract curve: one equation describing the entire family of efficient allocations, $0 \le x_A \le X$.

$$108\,y_A - 9x_Ay_A = 12x_A - x_Ay_A$$

$$y_A(108 - 8x_A) = 12x_A$$

$$\boxed{\ y_A = \frac{3x_A}{27 - 2x_A}\ }$$

Step 5Run the checks.

(a) The curve must run corner to corner: $x_A = 0 \Rightarrow y_A = 0$ and $x_A = X \Rightarrow y_A = Y$ ("give A nothing" and "give A everything" are both efficient). (b) Spot-check one interior point back in the original equation. (c) The bow direction should match the tastes — the curve bends toward the good the $x$-lover loves.

(a) $x_A=0$: $y_A = 0$ ✓   $x_A=12$: $y_A = \frac{36}{3} = 12$ ✓

(b) $x_A = 9$: $y_A = \frac{27}{9} = 3$; check MRSs there: $3\cdot\frac39 = 1$ and $\frac13\cdot\frac{9}{3} = 1$ ✓ equal.

(c) A loves $x$ $(a=\tfrac34)$, so efficient points load A with $x$ and the curve bows below the diagonal ✓

How the two algorithms fit together

Algorithm 2 never used the endowment — $\omega$ appears nowhere in it, which is why redistributing endowments never moves the contract curve. Algorithm 1 used $\omega$ in its very second step — which is why the equilibrium does move when $\omega$ does.

And here is the punchline you already verified without noticing: Algorithm 1's answer, $A = (9,3)$, sits exactly on Algorithm 2's curve — $\frac{3\cdot 9}{27-18} = 3$. That is the First Welfare Theorem (tab 6): the market-clearing algorithm always lands on the efficiency algorithm's curve. The endowment just decides where on it.

How to practice with this tab. Every practice problem on this sheet is a step from one of these two algorithms wearing a costume. When you get stuck, first ask "which algorithm?" (does the problem mention prices?), then "which step am I on?" — and reread just that row. And when a problem hands you different preferences (complements, substitutes, quasilinear), only the right column changes; the left columns are identical every single time.

1

Building the Edgeworth Box

The Edgeworth Box is a trick for putting two people's diagrams on one picture. It works because of feasibility: once you know what A has, you automatically know what B has, since $x_B = X - x_A$ and $y_B = Y - y_A$. One point can therefore describe the entire economy.

How to read any point in the box

What you wantWhere to look
$x_A$Horizontal distance from the bottom-left corner $O_A$
$y_A$Vertical distance from $O_A$
$x_B$Horizontal distance from the top-right corner $O_B$, measured leftward
$y_B$Vertical distance from $O_B$, measured downward

Trap #1, and it costs people whole problems. A gets happier moving up and to the right. B gets happier moving down and to the left — toward $O_B$'s origin, which sits in the top-right corner. Every time you look at one of B's indifference curves, remind yourself that "better for B" points at the opposite corner from "better for A." That opposition is the entire reason a lens exists.

2

The endowment, and the lens it opens

The endowment $\omega$ is one specific point in the box: $\omega = (4,8)$ in A's coordinates, which is automatically $(8,4)$ in B's. It is where the economy starts before anyone trades.

Now draw the indifference curve each person is on at $\omega$. Because A improves upward-right and B improves downward-left, the two curves cut through each other and carve out a lens-shaped region:

Why the lens is non-empty here. At $\omega$, A's marginal rate of substitution is

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{\alpha_A}{\beta_A}\cdot\frac{y_A}{x_A} = \frac{3/4}{1/4}\cdot\frac{8}{4} = 3\cdot 2 = 6,$$

and B's is

$$\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{\alpha_B}{\beta_B}\cdot\frac{y_B}{x_B} = \frac{1/4}{3/4}\cdot\frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac12 = \frac16 .$$

Read those in words. A would hand over 6 units of $y$ for one more unit of $x$. B would hand over only 1/6 of a unit of $y$ for the same thing — which is the same as saying B would happily sell a unit of $x$ for anything above $1/6$ of a unit of $y$.

So there is a range of exchange rates — anything strictly between $1/6$ and $6$ — at which A wants to buy $x$ and B wants to sell it, and both of them come out ahead. The lens is that range, drawn as an area.

The general rule you should be able to state instantly: whenever $\mathrm{MRS}_A \neq \mathrm{MRS}_B$, gains from trade exist, and the person with the higher MRS for $x$ should end up buying $x$. When the two MRSs are equal, the lens collapses to nothing and the trading is done.

Three things to try before you leave this tab

1. Drag the dot to roughly $(9,3)$. The lens vanishes and the two curves just touch. Note the MRS readouts.

2. Now drag to roughly $(6,1)$. The lens vanishes again — but $u_A$ is much lower than it was at $(9,3)$. Efficiency by itself says nothing about who wins.

3. Turn on the contract curve and drag along it. Every point on that curve is efficient; they differ only in how the gains are split.

1

Two definitions, stated precisely

Pareto improvement

A move from allocation $z$ to allocation $z'$ is a Pareto improvement if it makes at least one person strictly better off and nobody worse off.

Plain English: somebody wins and nobody loses.

Pareto optimal (= Pareto efficient)

A feasible allocation is Pareto optimal if no Pareto improvement is available from it. Formally: there is no other feasible $z'$ with $u_A(z') \ge u_A(z)$ and $u_B(z') \ge u_B(z)$, at least one strictly.

Plain English: you cannot help one without hurting the other.

Trap #2, the one graders love. "Pareto optimal" is a statement about waste, not about justice. In our box, the allocation where A gets all 12 units of both goods and B gets literally nothing is Pareto optimal — you cannot make B better off without taking something from A. Efficiency and fairness are different axes. Never write "efficient, therefore fair," and never write "unfair, therefore inefficient."

2

Why efficiency means tangency

0

The plan. We want to show that at an interior efficient allocation the two indifference curves must be tangent. The strategy is to prove the contrapositive: assume the curves cross at different slopes, then construct an explicit trade that helps both people. If such a trade always exists, crossing at different slopes cannot be efficient — so efficiency requires equal slopes.

1

Set up the disagreement. Suppose at some interior allocation $\mathrm{MRS}_A > \mathrm{MRS}_B$. By the definition of the marginal rate of substitution, $\mathrm{MRS}_A$ is the number of units of $y$ that A is just willing to give up for one more unit of $x$, and $\mathrm{MRS}_B$ is the number of units of $y$ that B must receive to part with one unit of $x$.

2

Find a price in between. Since $\mathrm{MRS}_A > \mathrm{MRS}_B$, pick any number $t$ strictly between them: $\mathrm{MRS}_B < t < \mathrm{MRS}_A$. Now execute the trade "A gives B a small amount $t\,\varepsilon$ of good $y$; B gives A a small amount $\varepsilon$ of good $x$."

3

Check both sides. A was willing to pay up to $\mathrm{MRS}_A \cdot \varepsilon$ units of $y$ and only paid $t\varepsilon < \mathrm{MRS}_A\varepsilon$, so A gains. B required at least $\mathrm{MRS}_B\cdot\varepsilon$ and received $t\varepsilon > \mathrm{MRS}_B \varepsilon$, so B gains. (Both statements are exact in the limit as $\varepsilon \to 0$, which is all we need for a marginal argument.)

4

Conclude. A Pareto improvement exists whenever the MRSs differ, so no allocation with differing MRSs is Pareto optimal. The same argument with the inequality reversed handles $\mathrm{MRS}_A < \mathrm{MRS}_B$. Therefore at any interior Pareto optimum:

$$\boxed{\ \mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B\ }$$

Geometrically: the two indifference curves through that point have the same slope, i.e. they are tangent, and the lens has been squeezed to nothing.

Read the word "interior." The argument used a small trade in both directions, which requires that both people already hold some of both goods. At a corner — someone holding zero of a good — the trade may be impossible and efficiency can hold with $\mathrm{MRS}_A \neq \mathrm{MRS}_B$. That is exactly what happens with perfect substitutes in tab 3.

3

Deriving the contract curve

The contract curve is the set of all Pareto optimal allocations, drawn inside the box. Finding it is a two-line recipe: write both MRSs in terms of A's coordinates alone, then set them equal.

1

Write A's MRS. For $u_A = x_A^{3/4}y_A^{1/4}$, the Cobb–Douglas shortcut gives

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{\partial u_A/\partial x_A}{\partial u_A/\partial y_A} = \frac{\alpha_A}{\beta_A}\cdot\frac{y_A}{x_A} = \frac{3/4}{1/4}\cdot\frac{y_A}{x_A} = 3\,\frac{y_A}{x_A}.$$
2

Write B's MRS — then translate it into A's coordinates. This substitution is the step people forget. For $u_B = x_B^{1/4}y_B^{3/4}$,

$$\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{\alpha_B}{\beta_B}\cdot\frac{y_B}{x_B} = \frac13\cdot\frac{y_B}{x_B} = \frac13\cdot\frac{12 - y_A}{12 - x_A},$$

using feasibility, $x_B = 12 - x_A$ and $y_B = 12 - y_A$.

3

Set them equal and clear the fractions.

$$3\,\frac{y_A}{x_A} = \frac13\cdot\frac{12-y_A}{12-x_A} \;\Longrightarrow\; 9\,y_A(12 - x_A) = x_A(12 - y_A)$$
4

Expand and collect the $y_A$ terms. Note that the $x_Ay_A$ terms do not cancel here — they combine:

$$108\,y_A - 9x_Ay_A = 12x_A - x_Ay_A \;\Longrightarrow\; 108\,y_A - 8x_Ay_A = 12x_A \;\Longrightarrow\; y_A\,(108 - 8x_A) = 12x_A$$
5

Solve for $y_A$. Divide by $(108-8x_A)$ and cancel a factor of 4:

$$\boxed{\ y_A = \frac{12x_A}{108 - 8x_A} = \frac{3x_A}{27 - 2x_A}, \qquad 0 \le x_A \le 12\ }$$

Sanity checks, always run at least two. At $x_A = 0$: $y_A = 0$, so the curve starts at $O_A$. At $x_A = 12$: $y_A = 36/3 = 12$, so it ends at $O_B$. At $x_A = 9$: $y_A = 27/9 = 3$ — remember that point, it comes back in tab 5. And the curve sits below the diagonal, which is what it should do: A cares more about $x$, so efficient allocations load A up on $x$ and B up on $y$.

Want to run this derivation with your hands instead of algebra? The ✦ Derivation Lab tab has a slider that freezes A's utility, finds B's tangency, and traces the curve out point by point — with a movable endowment so you can watch what depends on ω and what does not.

The general Cobb–Douglas formula (worth carrying)

For $u_A = x^{\alpha_A}y^{\beta_A}$ and $u_B = x^{\alpha_B}y^{\beta_B}$ with totals $X$ and $Y$, only the exponent ratios matter. Write $r_A = \frac{\alpha_A}{\beta_A}$ and $r_B = \frac{\alpha_B}{\beta_B}$ (for our example, $r_A = 3$ and $r_B = \frac13$). Running the same five steps in symbols gives

$$y_A = \frac{r_B\,Y\,x_A}{r_A X - (r_A-r_B)x_A}$$

Two special cases are worth recognizing on sight:

• If $r_A = r_B$ (identical tastes — the exponents need not match, only their ratio) this collapses to $y_A = \frac{Y}{X}x_A$ — the contract curve is the straight diagonal of the box.

• If $r_A > r_B$, A weights $x$ more heavily and the curve bows below the diagonal (our case). If $r_A < r_B$ it bows above.

Trap #3. The contract curve depends only on preferences and totals. It does not move when you change the endowment. What the endowment changes is which point on the curve the market lands on — because it changes who is rich. Students who redraw the contract curve after a redistribution have lost the plot; students who redraw the price line have understood it.

Side note you may hear in lecture: the core. Not every efficient allocation is one that both people would agree to. Nobody accepts a deal that leaves them worse off than simply keeping their endowment. The part of the contract curve lying inside the original lens — efficient and at least as good as $\omega$ for both — is called the core. It is the set of deals that are both waste-free and voluntary. The competitive equilibrium always lands inside it.

✦

Watch the contract curve get derived

Tab 2 • Pareto & Contract Curve derived the contract curve with algebra. This tab derives it with your hands, running the actual experiment the algebra is shorthand for:

The experiment. Freeze A on one indifference curve — she is not allowed to get any worse off than that. Now make B as happy as possible. B climbs from curve to curve until his indifference curve just kisses A's frozen one: a tangency. That stopping point is one point of the contract curve. Raise A's frozen level a little and repeat — you get the next point. The contract curve is nothing but the trail this experiment leaves behind as A's level sweeps from "A has almost nothing" to "A has almost everything."

The slider below is that sweep — but each stop only shows you the experiment's finished answer. To watch the experiment itself happen, press ▶ run the experiment: A's green curve holds perfectly still (she is the frozen one), and B's copper curve visibly climbs, sweeping toward A until it just kisses her curve and has to stop. That stopping point is the tangency. Then nudge the slider and run it again at a new level.

The green curve is A's frozen indifference curve; the copper curve is B's; the dashed line at rest is their common tangent, whose slope is the shared MRS.

…or just drag the white square anywhere in the box.

Three experiments to run before you leave

1. Trace the whole curve. Sweep the slider from far left to far right, slowly. Watch the MRS readout as you go: it is different at every point, but at each stop it is shared — that is what makes every point on the trail efficient. Notice the trail runs corner to corner: at the far left A has almost nothing, at the far right almost everything, and both extremes are still "efficient."

2. Move ω and watch what does not move. Drag the endowment all over the box, or flip between the presets. The trail never budges — the contract curve is built from preferences and totals only. What moves is everything else: the lens, the gold core segment, and the CE dot. This is Trap #3 from tab 2, live.

3. Find the deals nobody would sign. Park the tangency outside the gold segment and read the verdict: the point is efficient, yet one person is worse off there than at ω and would simply refuse to trade. Efficient does not mean acceptable. The gold stretch — efficient and at least as good as ω for both — is the core, and the CE always lands inside it.

The bridge back to the algebra. "B's curve just kisses A's frozen curve" is the sentence; $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$ is the same sentence in symbols. Solving that equation for $y_A$ in terms of $x_A$ (the five steps in tab 2 • Pareto & Contract Curve) computes the entire trail at once instead of one slider-stop at a time. The algebra is the sweep, done in a single line.

1

Same box, four preference worlds

Everything in tab 2 assumed smooth, convex, interior tangency. That is the Cobb–Douglas world, and it is only one of the four preference types you already know. The box itself does not care — it is just bookkeeping — but the shape of the contract curve changes completely, and so does whether the tangency rule even applies.

To make the comparison honest, all four worlds below use the same box and the same endowment: $X = Y = 12$, $\omega_A = (4,8)$, $\omega_B = (8,4)$. Only the utility functions change.

Type 1 — Cobb–Douglas: the smooth bowed curve

CONCEPT

$u_A = x^{3/4}y^{1/4}$, $u_B = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$. Smooth, strictly convex, and both goods are always wanted, so every optimum is interior and the tangency rule applies exactly as derived.

Contract curve: $y_A = \dfrac{3x_A}{27-2x_A}$  —  a smooth arc from $O_A$ to $O_B$, bowed toward the $x$-axis because A is the $x$-lover.

Equilibrium: $p^* = 1$, $A = (9,3)$, $B = (3,9)$.

Setup. Let $u_A = x^{\alpha_A}y^{\beta_A}$ and $u_B = x^{\alpha_B}y^{\beta_B}$, with taste ratios $r_A = \frac{\alpha_A}{\beta_A}$ and $r_B = \frac{\alpha_B}{\beta_B}$, and totals $X$, $Y$.

1. Write both MRSs in A's coordinates (feasibility: $x_B = X - x_A$, $y_B = Y - y_A$):

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = r_A\,\frac{y_A}{x_A}, \qquad \mathrm{MRS}_B = r_B\,\frac{Y - y_A}{X - x_A}.$$

2. Efficiency is tangency — set them equal and cross-multiply:

$$r_A\,y_A\,(X - x_A) = r_B\,x_A\,(Y - y_A).$$

3. Expand, collect the $y_A$ terms, and factor:

$$y_A\left[\,r_A X - (r_A - r_B)\,x_A\,\right] = r_B\,Y\,x_A$$
$$\boxed{\ y_A = \frac{r_B\,Y\,x_A}{r_A X - (r_A - r_B)\,x_A}\ }$$

A smooth arc from $O_A$ to $O_B$; it bows toward the axis of whichever good the higher-$r$ person loves.

Given: $u_A = x^{2/3}y^{1/3}$, $u_B = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$, $X = Y = 10$. So $r_A = \frac{2/3}{1/3} = 2$ and $r_B = \frac{1/2}{1/2} = 1$.

Step 2: $\ 2\,\frac{y_A}{x_A} = \frac{10 - y_A}{10 - x_A} \Rightarrow 2y_A(10 - x_A) = x_A(10 - y_A)$.

Step 3: $\ 20y_A - 2x_Ay_A = 10x_A - x_Ay_A \Rightarrow y_A(20 - x_A) = 10x_A$:

$$y_A = \frac{10\,x_A}{20 - x_A}$$

Checks: $x_A = 0 \Rightarrow y_A = 0$ ✓; $x_A = 10 \Rightarrow y_A = \frac{100}{10} = 10$ ✓ (corner to corner). Spot-check $x_A = 4$: $y_A = \frac{40}{16} = 2.5$, and there $\mathrm{MRS}_A = 2\cdot\frac{2.5}{4} = 1.25$ while $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{7.5}{6} = 1.25$ ✓ equal. And since $r_A = 2 > 1 = r_B$, the curve bows below the diagonal, toward the $x$-lover ✓

This is the default case and the one to assume when a problem does not say otherwise.

Type 2 — Perfect complements: the diagonal, and a price that refuses to be pinned down

CONCEPT

$u_A = \min(x_A,y_A)$, $u_B = \min(x_B,y_B)$. Indifference curves are L-shaped. At the kink the MRS is undefined — the curve has no slope there — so "set $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$" is not available. You must reason directly from the definition of efficiency.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Finding the Pareto set without tangency. Suppose an allocation is off the diagonal, say $A = (6,7)$ and therefore $B = (6,5)$. Then $u_A = \min(6,7) = 6$ and $u_B = \min(6,5) = 5$. A's seventh unit of $y$ is doing nothing for A — it is past the kink. Hand it to B: now $A = (6,6)$ with $u_A = 6$ (unchanged) and $B=(6,6)$ with $u_B = 6$ (up). That is a Pareto improvement, so the original point was not efficient.

The same argument kills every off-diagonal point. What survives is exactly the set where both people sit at their kinks: $x_A = y_A$ and $x_B = y_B$.

Contract curve: the straight diagonal from $O_A$ to $O_B$, i.e. $y_A = x_A$.

Equilibrium: demand is $x_i = y_i = \dfrac{m_i}{p+1}$, so total demand for $x$ is $\dfrac{m_A + m_B}{p+1} = \dfrac{12p+12}{p+1} = 12$ for every $p$. Every positive price clears both markets.

What that actually means. There is not one equilibrium here but a whole family of them, one per price ratio, sliding along the diagonal: $p=1$ gives $A=(6,6)$; $p=3$ gives $A=(5,5)$ and $B=(7,7)$. All are efficient; they differ in who captures the gains. Uniqueness of equilibrium is a conclusion that needs strictly convex preferences, not a law of nature. (Related edge case: if the totals were unequal, say $X=12$ but $Y=18$, the extra 6 units of $y$ would be worthless to everyone and equilibrium would require $p_y = 0$ — $y$ becomes a free good.)

Setup. $u_A = \min(x_A, y_A)$, $u_B = \min(x_B, y_B)$, equal totals $X = Y$. The MRS is undefined at the kinks, so we argue straight from the definition of efficiency.

1. Take any allocation where A is off her kink, say $y_A > x_A$. Then $u_A = x_A$: the surplus $y_A - x_A$ contributes nothing to A.

2. Hand that surplus $y$ to B. A's utility is unchanged ($u_A = x_A$ still); B's holding of $y$ rises, so $u_B = \min(x_B, y_B)$ either rises or stays the same — and because $X = Y$, one can show B was $y$-short whenever A is $y$-long, so it strictly rises.

3. A Pareto improvement existed, so the original point was not efficient. The same argument kills $x_A > y_A$ (hand the surplus $x$ to B). What survives is exactly:

$$\boxed{\ x_A = y_A \quad (\text{and hence } x_B = y_B) \ }$$

— both people sitting on their kinks: the diagonal of the box.

Given: $X = Y = 10$ and the allocation $A = (4, 6)$, so $B = (6, 4)$.

Utilities: $u_A = \min(4,6) = 4$ and $u_B = \min(6,4) = 4$. A's 2 extra units of $y$ are doing nothing.

The improving move: transfer those 2 units of $y$ to B. Now $A = (4,4)$: $u_A = 4$, unchanged. $B = (6,6)$: $u_B = 6$, up from 4. Somebody gained, nobody lost — so $(4,6)$ was not efficient.

And the endpoint is untouchable: at $A = (4,4)$, $B = (6,6)$, try to help B further: any $x$ or $y$ taken from A drops $u_A$ below 4 immediately (she has no slack), and B cannot be helped with nothing. On the diagonal, no free improvements remain — efficient.

Type 3 — Perfect substitutes: efficiency on the edges

CONCEPT

$u_A = 2x_A + y_A$ and $u_B = x_B + 2y_B$. Indifference curves are straight lines, so $\mathrm{MRS}_A = 2$ and $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac12$ everywhere, no matter what anyone holds. The two constants are never equal, so an interior tangency literally cannot exist — and yet efficient allocations obviously do exist. This is the case the "interior" caveat in tab 2 was warning you about.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Since $\mathrm{MRS}_A > \mathrm{MRS}_B$ always, A always values $x$ more at the margin, so any interior point can be improved by shipping $x$ toward A and $y$ toward B. That process only stops when it cannot continue — when A has all the $x$ there is $(x_A = 12)$, or B has all the $y$ there is $(y_A = 0)$.

Check one: at $A = (12,5)$, for both to gain, A must receive more than $2$ units of $y$ per unit of $x$ surrendered while B must pay less than $\frac12$. Impossible — so it is efficient even though the MRSs differ.

Pareto set: the right edge $x_A = 12$ together with the bottom edge $y_A = 0$ — an L, not a curve.

Equilibrium: A buys only $x$ whenever $p < 2$, B buys only $y$ whenever $p > \frac12$. Guess an equilibrium in that window: A's income is $4p + 8$, all spent on $x$, so $x_A = \frac{4p+8}{p} = 12 \Rightarrow p^* = 1$. Then $A = (12,0)$, $B = (0,12)$, and $u_A$ rises from $16$ to $24$ while $u_B$ does the same.

Setup. $u_A = a\,x_A + b\,y_A$ and $u_B = c\,x_B + d\,y_B$: straight-line indifference curves with constant $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac ab$ and $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac cd$. Suppose $\frac ab > \frac cd$ (A values $x$ more, everywhere and always).

1. Take any interior allocation — both people holding some of both goods. Pick a trade rate $t$ with $\frac cd < t < \frac ab$: B sells A one unit of $x$ for $t$ units of $y$.

2. A pays $t < \frac ab$ for something she values at $\frac ab$ — she gains. B receives $t > \frac cd$ for something he values at $\frac cd$ — he gains. Both improved, so the interior point was not efficient.

3. Because the MRSs are constants, this argument never switches off as trade proceeds — there is no convergence. It only stops when the trade becomes physically impossible: A holds all the $x$ ($x_A = X$), or B holds all the $y$ ($y_A = 0$).

$$\boxed{\ \text{Pareto set} = \{x_A = X\} \cup \{y_A = 0\}\ }$$

— the right edge together with the bottom edge: an L, not a curve.

Given: $u_A = 2x + y$, $u_B = x + 2y$, $X = Y = 12$, and the interior allocation $A = (6,6)$, $B = (6,6)$. MRSs: $2$ versus $\frac12$ — pick the in-between rate $t = 1$.

One round of trade (one $x$ to A for one $y$ to B): $A = (7,5)$: $u_A = 14+5 = 19$, up from $18$ ✓. $B = (5,7)$: $u_B = 5+14 = 19$, up from $18$ ✓.

Keep going — the MRSs never budge ($2$ and $\frac12$ at every step), so the same trade keeps working: $(8,4), (9,3), \ldots$ all the way to $A = (12,0)$, $B = (0,12)$, where $u_A = 24$ and $u_B = 24$.

Why it stops there: to improve B now you must give him $x$; A demands at least $2$ units of $y$ per unit of $x$, but B will pay at most $\frac12$. No rate works — the corner is efficient even though $\mathrm{MRS}_A \neq \mathrm{MRS}_B$.

The reflex to build: linear preferences $\Rightarrow$ compare the constant MRS to the price ratio $\Rightarrow$ expect a corner. Setting two constants equal to each other is a wasted line of algebra.

Type 4 — Quasilinear: the vertical contract curve

CONCEPT

$u_A = 8\ln x_A + y_A$ and $u_B = 4\ln x_B + y_B$. Good $y$ enters linearly, so $\mathrm{MRS}_A = 8/x_A$ depends on $x_A$ only. The indifference curves are vertical shifts of one another — move up and you get a parallel copy.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Efficiency requires $\dfrac{8}{x_A} = \dfrac{4}{x_B} = \dfrac{4}{12 - x_A}$. Cross-multiplying, $8(12-x_A) = 4x_A$, so $96 = 12x_A$ and $x_A = 8$. Notice what did not appear anywhere in that calculation: $y_A$.

Contract curve: the vertical line $x_A = 8$ — efficiency pins down the split of $x$ completely and says nothing at all about the split of $y$.

Equilibrium: $\mathrm{MRS}_A = p \Rightarrow x_A = 8/p$ and $x_B = 4/p$; clearing gives $12/p = 12$, so $p^* = 1$, $A = (8,4)$, $B=(4,8)$.

Setup. $u_A = \alpha\ln x_A + y_A$ and $u_B = \beta\ln x_B + y_B$, totals $X$ and $Y$. The linear $y$ term makes each MRS depend on $x$ only:

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{\alpha}{x_A}, \qquad \mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{\beta}{x_B} = \frac{\beta}{X - x_A}.$$

1. Tangency (both smooth and interior in $x$):

$$\frac{\alpha}{x_A} = \frac{\beta}{X - x_A}$$

2. Cross-multiply and solve — notice $y_A$ never appears:

$$\alpha(X - x_A) = \beta\,x_A \;\Longrightarrow\; \alpha X = (\alpha+\beta)\,x_A$$
$$\boxed{\ x_A = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\,X \quad\text{for every value of } y_A\ }$$

One equation, one unknown, and $y_A$ free: a vertical line. Efficiency pins down the split of $x$ completely and says nothing about the split of $y$ — moving $y$ between the two people slides you up and down the line without leaving it.

Given: $u_A = 6\ln x_A + y_A$, $u_B = 2\ln x_B + y_B$, $X = 8$ (and any $Y$).

Step 1: $\ \dfrac{6}{x_A} = \dfrac{2}{8 - x_A}$.

Step 2: $\ 6(8 - x_A) = 2x_A \Rightarrow 48 = 8x_A \Rightarrow x_A = 6$ (matching the formula: $\frac{6}{6+2}\cdot 8 = 6$).

$$\text{Contract curve: the vertical line } x_A = 6,\ x_B = 2$$

Check: $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac66 = 1$ and $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac22 = 1$ ✓ — and both stay equal to 1 no matter how the $y$ is divided, which is exactly why every $y$-split along $x_A = 6$ is efficient.

This is why quasilinear preferences are the workhorse of applied welfare analysis: the efficient quantity of $x$ is a single number independent of distribution, so you can talk about "the efficient level" without first arguing about who should be rich. Redistribution moves you up and down the line, never off it.

One table to hold all four

PreferencesEfficient set in the boxMethod that worksWhat to watch for

1

The budget line has to go through $\omega$

In partial equilibrium your budget constraint was $p_x x + p_y y = m$ with $m$ given. Here nobody hands you $m$. Your income is whatever your endowment is worth at current prices:

$$p_x x_A + p_y y_A = \underbrace{p_x \omega_{Ax} + p_y \omega_{Ay}}_{\text{value of what A already owns}}$$

With the normalization $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$, this is $\ px_A + y_A = p\,\omega_{Ax} + \omega_{Ay}$.

Two consequences fall straight out of that equation, and they drive everything in this tab:

(i) The line always passes through $\omega$. Plug $(x_A,y_A) = \omega_A$ into the constraint and both sides are identical. "Do nothing" is always affordable — which is exactly why nobody can be forced into a trade that hurts them.

(ii) Changing $p$ pivots the line around $\omega$ rather than shifting it in and out. A price change does not just change what you can buy; it changes how rich you are. That is a genuinely new effect with no counterpart in the fixed-income problem.

Where this shows up on tests. A rise in $p_x$ makes the $x$-owner richer and the $x$-buyer poorer. So the income effect of a price change has a sign that depends on which side of the market you are on — an endowment effect that partial equilibrium simply does not have.

2

Gross demand, net demand, excess demand

Three phrases that sound alike and are not. Keep them straight and half the confusion in this unit disappears.

TermDefinitionIn the running example at $p=1$
Gross demand$x_A$ — the total amount A wants to end up holding$x_A = 9$
Net demand$x_A - \omega_{Ax}$ — how much A wants to buy (negative = sell)$9 - 4 = +5$: A buys 5 units of $x$
Excess demand$z_x(p) = x_A + x_B - X$ — the whole market's net demand$9 + 3 - 12 = 0$: the market clears

Equilibrium is a statement about the third row: a price $p^*$ at which excess demand is zero in every market. Individual net demands can be enormous; they just have to cancel.

What a wrong price looks like

Set $p = 1.5$ in the running example. Both people optimize honestly against the same line through $\omega$ — and they choose points that are not the same point, which is precisely what "the market does not clear" means.

3

Offer curves: every choice at every price, on one line

An offer curve (also called a price–offer curve) traces a single person's optimal bundle as the price ratio sweeps from $0$ to $\infty$. It is a cousin of the demand curves you built earlier in the summer — the same idea of choice-as-a-function-of-price — with one genuinely new feature: income moves as the price moves, because income is endowment value.

1

A's income at price $p$. $m_A(p) = p\cdot 4 + 8 = 4p + 8$.

2

Apply the Cobb–Douglas share rule — spend the exponent share $\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}$ of income on $x$ (here $\frac{3/4}{3/4+1/4} = \frac34$) and the rest on $y$:

$$x_A(p) = \frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{4p+8}{p} = 3 + \frac{6}{p}, \qquad y_A(p) = \frac14 (4p+8) = p + 2.$$
3

Eliminate $p$ to get the curve itself. From the second equation $p = y_A - 2$; substituting,

$$x_A = 3 + \frac{6}{y_A - 2}, \qquad y_A > 2.$$
4

Do the same for B. $m_B(p) = 8p+4$, and B spends $\frac14$ of it on $x$:

$$x_B(p) = 2 + \frac{1}{p}, \qquad y_B(p) = 6p + 3.$$

Two facts that make offer curves easy to sanity-check.

• Every offer curve passes through $\omega$. Set $x_A(p) = 4$: then $3 + 6/p = 4$ gives $p = 6$, and $y_A(6) = 8$. So at $p = 6$ A voluntarily chooses to hold exactly her endowment. That price is A's autarky price — the exchange rate at which she is unwilling to trade at all. It equals her MRS at $\omega$, which we computed in tab 1 as $6$. That is not a coincidence; it is the tangency condition.

• B's autarky price is $p = 1/6$, again equal to $\mathrm{MRS}_B$ at $\omega$. The equilibrium price must lie between the two autarky prices — here between $1/6$ and $6$ — because outside that range both people want to be on the same side of the market.

4

Walras' Law — and why you only ever solve one market

0

The plan. Add up the two budget constraints and see what falls out. Nothing else is needed — no optimization, no preferences, just the fact that everyone spends exactly their income.

1

Write both budget constraints as equalities. With locally non-satiated preferences (more is better), no one leaves money unspent:

$$p\,x_A + y_A = p\,\omega_{Ax} + \omega_{Ay}, \qquad p\,x_B + y_B = p\,\omega_{Bx} + \omega_{By}.$$
2

Add them. Group the $x$ terms and the $y$ terms:

$$p\,(x_A + x_B) + (y_A + y_B) = p\,X + Y.$$
3

Move everything to one side and recognize the excess demand functions $z_x = x_A+x_B-X$ and $z_y = y_A+y_B-Y$:

$$\boxed{\ p\,z_x(p) + z_y(p) = 0 \quad \text{for every } p\ }$$

The total value of excess demand across all markets is zero at every price, not just the equilibrium one.

4

The payoff. If $z_x(p^*) = 0$ and $p^* > 0$, the identity forces $z_y(p^*) = 0$. With two goods, clearing one market clears the other automatically. So you solve one equation, not two — and then use the second market as a free check on your algebra.

See it in our numbers. $z_x(p) = \left(3+\frac6p\right) + \left(2+\frac1p\right) - 12 = \dfrac{7}{p} - 7$ and $z_y(p) = (p+2)+(6p+3) - 12 = 7p - 7$. Then

$$p\,z_x + z_y = p\left(\frac7p - 7\right) + 7p - 7 = 7 - 7p + 7p - 7 = 0.\ \checkmark$$

Both vanish at $p = 1$, as they must. Note also that $z_x$ is falling in $p$ and $z_y$ is rising — excess demand for a good falls as its own price rises, which is what makes the equilibrium stable.

1

The definition, in three conditions

A competitive (Walrasian) equilibrium for an exchange economy is a price ratio $p^*$ together with an allocation $\big((x_A^*,y_A^*),(x_B^*,y_B^*)\big)$ such that:

(1) Optimization. Each person's bundle maximizes their own utility subject to their own endowment-valued budget constraint, taking $p^*$ as given.

(2) Feasibility / market clearing. $x_A^* + x_B^* = X$ and $y_A^* + y_B^* = Y$.

(3) Price taking. Nobody believes their own choices move $p^*$. (This is an assumption about behavior, not an equation you solve — but it is what makes the model "competitive," and it is exactly the assumption that fails in the monopoly and Cournot models you already know.)

Trap #4. Condition (1) is not "the bundle is affordable." Affordable is easy; optimal is the requirement. An allocation can sit exactly on both budget lines and still fail to be an equilibrium because someone would rather be somewhere else on that same line. Practice problem 8 is built entirely on this distinction.

2

The five-step recipe

Step 1 — Normalize. Set $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$. One unknown price, not two.

Step 2 — Write each income as endowment value. $m_A = p\,\omega_{Ax} + \omega_{Ay}$, and the same for B. This is the step that separates general from partial equilibrium; do it explicitly every single time.

Step 3 — Get each person's demand as a function of $p$. Use whatever demand rule the utility function calls for — the Cobb–Douglas share rule, the complements ratio, a corner comparison for substitutes, or $\mathrm{MRS} = p$ for quasilinear.

Step 4 — Clear one market. Set $x_A(p) + x_B(p) = X$ and solve the single equation for $p^*$. Walras' Law guarantees the other market is then clear too.

Step 5 — Substitute back and check. Plug $p^*$ into the demands to get the allocation, then verify: (a) the other market clears, (b) each person's budget balances, and (c) both people are at least as well off as at $\omega$.

3

Worked example 1 — the running economy

Given: $u_A = x^{3/4}y^{1/4}$ with $\omega_A = (4,8)$; $u_B = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$ with $\omega_B = (8,4)$; $X = Y = 12$.

1

Normalize: $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$.

2

Incomes: $m_A = 4p + 8$ and $m_B = 8p + 4$.

3

Demands, by the share rule:

$$x_A = \frac34\cdot\frac{4p+8}{p} = 3+\frac6p, \qquad x_B = \frac14\cdot\frac{8p+4}{p} = 2+\frac1p.$$
4

Clear the $x$ market:

$$3+\frac6p+2+\frac1p = 12 \;\Longrightarrow\; 5 + \frac7p = 12 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac7p = 7 \;\Longrightarrow\; p^* = 1.$$
5

Substitute back: $x_A = 9$, $y_A = \frac14(4+8) = 3$, $x_B = 3$, $y_B = \frac34(8+4) = 9$.

$$\boxed{\ p^* = 1,\qquad A = (9,3),\qquad B = (3,9)\ }$$

All three checks:

• Other market: $y_A + y_B = 3 + 9 = 12 = Y$. ✓

• A's budget: spends $1(9) + 3 = 12$; income $1(4)+8 = 12$. ✓ (A's net demand is $+5$ units of $x$ and $-5$ units of $y$: she buys 5 $x$ and pays with 5 $y$. B's net demands are the mirror image, which is what clearing means.)

• Gains: $u_A$ goes from $4^{3/4}8^{1/4} = 4.76$ to $9^{3/4}3^{1/4} = 6.84$; $u_B$ goes from $4.76$ to $6.84$ as well. Both strictly better off. ✓

• Bonus check: is $(9,3)$ on the contract curve $y_A = \frac{3x_A}{27-2x_A}$? $\frac{27}{27-18} = \frac{27}{9} = 3$. ✓ That is the First Welfare Theorem showing up in your arithmetic.

Do not read anything into $p^* = 1$. The numbers in this example were chosen symmetrically so the algebra stays clean. Equilibrium prices are usually not $1$ — see the next example, and every practice problem.

4

Worked example 2 — a lopsided economy, $p^* \neq 1$

Given: $u_A = x^{2/3}y^{1/3}$ with $\omega_A = (6,0)$; $u_B = x^{1/3}y^{2/3}$ with $\omega_B = (0,12)$. So $X = 6$ and $Y = 12$: A owns all the $x$, B owns all the $y$, and each wants what the other has.

1–2

Normalize and write incomes: $m_A = 6p + 0 = 6p$ and $m_B = 0 + 12 = 12$. Notice A's income rises with $p$ and B's does not — A is the seller of $x$.

3

Demands:

$$x_A = \frac23\cdot\frac{6p}{p} = 4 \quad(\text{constant!}), \qquad x_B = \frac13\cdot\frac{12}{p} = \frac4p.$$

A's demand for $x$ does not depend on $p$ at all: a higher price makes $x$ more expensive but makes A exactly proportionally richer, and for Cobb–Douglas those two effects cancel when the endowment is all in that good.

4

Clear the $x$ market: $\;4 + \dfrac4p = 6 \Rightarrow \dfrac4p = 2 \Rightarrow p^* = 2$.

5

Substitute: $x_A = 4$, $y_A = \frac13(6\cdot 2) = 4$; $x_B = 2$, $y_B = \frac23(12) = 8$.

$$\boxed{\ p^* = 2,\qquad A = (4,4),\qquad B = (2,8)\ }$$

Checks: $y_A + y_B = 4 + 8 = 12$ ✓. A's budget: $2(4) + 4 = 12 = 2(6)$ ✓. Gains: $u_A$ rises from $6^{2/3}\cdot 0^{1/3} = 0$ to $4$, and $u_B$ from $0$ to $2^{1/3}8^{2/3} \approx 5.04$ ✓ — when you start with none of one good, Cobb–Douglas utility is zero, so any trade is a huge improvement.

Reading $p^* = 2$: one unit of $x$ trades for two units of $y$. That makes sense: $x$ is the scarcer good ($X = 6$ versus $Y = 12$), and scarcity shows up in the price.

5

Where marks actually get lost

The errorWhat it looks likeThe fix
Treating income as fixedWriting $x_A = \frac{3}{4}\frac{m}{p}$ with a number for $m$$m$ is always $p\omega_x + \omega_y$; it moves when $p$ moves
Forgetting to normalizeTwo unknown prices, one equation, stuckSet $p_y = 1$ in line one, every time
Solving both marketsTwo equations that turn out to be the same equationSolve one, use the other as a check (Walras)
Using totals as incomeSetting $m_A = pX + Y$That is the value of the whole economy, not of A's endowment
Reporting only $p^*$Answer stops at the priceAn equilibrium is a price and an allocation — report all four quantities
Assuming interior tangencySetting $\mathrm{MRS}=p$ for perfect substitutesCheck the preference type first (tab 3)
1

The First Welfare Theorem

First Welfare Theorem. If preferences are locally non-satiated (more is always better somewhere nearby), then every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto optimal.

This is the formal version of the invisible hand, and its reach is remarkable: no planner, no coordination, no one even trying to be efficient. Each person selfishly optimizes against a single number, and waste vanishes.

Why it is true — the one-line version

1

Each person's tangency condition. At an interior equilibrium, A optimizes, so A's indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: $\mathrm{MRS}_A = p$. B faces the same price, so $\mathrm{MRS}_B = p$ too.

2

Chain them. Two quantities equal to the same thing are equal to each other:

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = p = \mathrm{MRS}_B \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B,$$

which is precisely the efficiency condition from tab 2. So the equilibrium allocation is on the contract curve.

The mechanism in words. The price is a single public number that everyone's private marginal valuation is pushed against. Prices do not find the efficient point; they synchronize marginal valuations, and synchronized marginal valuations are what efficiency is.

The general proof does not even need calculus or tangency. Suppose some feasible allocation $z'$ made both people at least as well off, one strictly. Anything strictly better than what A chose must have been unaffordable at $p^*$ (or she would have bought it), and anything weakly better must cost at least as much. Adding up across people, $z'$ costs strictly more than the endowment is worth — so it is not feasible. Contradiction. That argument survives kinks, corners, and non-differentiable utility, which is why the theorem is stated with local non-satiation rather than smoothness.

What the First Welfare Theorem does not say — write this in the margin of your notes.

• It does not say the outcome is fair. Start A with everything and the equilibrium is "A keeps everything," which is efficient and grotesque.

• It does not say the outcome is unique. There can be several equilibria, and each of them is efficient.

• It does not survive externalities, public goods, market power, asymmetric information, or missing markets. Every one of those breaks the step where both people face the same price for the same marginal effect — and, not coincidentally, each is a later topic in this course. This theorem is the benchmark those topics are measured against.

2

The Second Welfare Theorem

Second Welfare Theorem. If in addition preferences are convex, then for any Pareto optimal allocation $z^*$ there exist prices $p^*$ and a redistribution of endowments such that $z^*$ is a competitive equilibrium of the redistributed economy.

Read it as the converse of the first. The First says markets get you onto the contract curve. The Second says markets can get you onto any point you like on that curve — provided you are willing to move the starting endowments first.

Why this is the politically interesting one. It separates the efficiency question from the distribution question. You do not have to choose between "let the market run" and "get the distribution you want." Redistribute the endowments, then let the market run: you get your distributional target and efficiency. Equity and efficiency stop being a trade-off — on paper.

The three-step recipe (and a worked example)

Take the quasilinear world from tab 3: $u_A = 8\ln x_A + y_A$, $u_B = 4\ln x_B + y_B$, $X = Y = 12$, $\omega_A = (4,8)$. Its contract curve is the vertical line $x_A = 8$. Suppose a planner wants the efficient allocation $A = (8,8)$, $B = (4,4)$ — the same efficient split of $x$ as the market gives, but with A holding much more $y$.

1

Find the supporting price. At the target, the common MRS is the required price ratio:

$$p^* = \mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{8}{x_A} = \frac{8}{8} = 1 \quad\text{(and } \mathrm{MRS}_B = \tfrac{4}{4} = 1 \text{, consistent }\checkmark).$$
2

Price the target and the current endowment. At $p^*=1$, the target bundle costs A $\;1(8) + 8 = 16$, while A's current endowment is worth only $1(4) + 8 = 12$.

3

Transfer the difference — lump sum. A needs 4 more units of income, so move 4 units of $y$ from B to A before the market opens: $\omega'_A = (4,12)$, $\omega'_B = (8,0)$. Now A's income is 16 and B's is 8.

Verify that the market now delivers the target on its own. At $p=1$: A chooses $x_A = 8/p = 8$ and then $y_A = 16 - 8 = 8$. ✓ B chooses $x_B = 4/p = 4$ and $y_B = 8 - 4 = 4$. ✓ Markets clear: $8+4 = 12$ and $8+4=12$. ✓ Nobody was ordered to do anything — the planner moved the starting point and the price did the rest.

Two conditions people skate past

Convexity is not decoration. The theorem needs a straight line that separates "better for A" from "better for B" at the target point. If an indifference curve is bowed the wrong way — non-convex preferences — the budget line through the target can leave a bundle on the same line that the consumer strictly prefers, so they will not choose the target and no price supports it. Some Pareto optima then simply cannot be decentralized. The First Welfare Theorem needs no such assumption; the Second does.

"Lump-sum" is doing enormous work. The transfer must not depend on anything the person can change. Real taxes are levied on income, on purchases, on wages — all of which are choices — so real taxes drive a wedge between the buyer's price and the seller's price, and the moment that happens, $\mathrm{MRS}_A \neq \mathrm{MRS}_B$ and the First Welfare Theorem's chain breaks. That gap between the elegant theorem and available policy instruments is where most of public economics lives.

3

The two theorems side by side

First Welfare TheoremSecond Welfare Theorem
DirectionEquilibrium $\Rightarrow$ efficientEfficient $\Rightarrow$ can be made an equilibrium
GivenA price and an allocation the market producedA target allocation on the contract curve
You must findNothing — it is already efficientSupporting prices and the required transfer
AssumptionsLocal non-satiation, price taking, no externalitiesAll of those plus convexity plus lump-sum transfers
EndowmentsLeft aloneDeliberately moved first
Exam phrasing"Show the CE is Pareto optimal""Find prices and transfers supporting this allocation"

If you remember one sentence from this tab: the market chooses a point on the contract curve, and the endowment chooses which point. The First Welfare Theorem is the first half of that sentence; the Second is the second half.

P

Practice — nine problems, in parts

Every problem is broken into lettered parts, and each part has its own solution toggle. Do a part, check it, then move on — do not read ahead. If a part takes more than a couple of minutes, that is the exact spot to reread the relevant tab.

Problems 1–4 build technique. Problems 5–7 are exam-shaped. Problems 8–9 are the conceptual traps.

1

Contract curve with identical tastes. $u_A = x_A^{1/2}y_A^{1/2}$ and $u_B = x_B^{1/2}y_B^{1/2}$. Totals: $X = 20$, $Y = 10$.

a Write $\mathrm{MRS}_A$ in terms of $x_A$ and $y_A$.

For $x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$ the shortcut is $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\cdot\frac{y}{x}$. Here $\alpha = \beta = \frac12$.

$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \dfrac{1/2}{1/2}\cdot\dfrac{y_A}{x_A} = \dfrac{y_A}{x_A}$.

b Write $\mathrm{MRS}_B$ — then convert it into A's coordinates.

Feasibility: $x_B = 20 - x_A$ and $y_B = 10 - y_A$. Skipping this substitution is the single most common error on this type.

$\mathrm{MRS}_B = \dfrac{y_B}{x_B} = \dfrac{10 - y_A}{20 - x_A}$.

c Set them equal and solve for $y_A$ as a function of $x_A$.

$\dfrac{y_A}{x_A} = \dfrac{10-y_A}{20-x_A} \Rightarrow y_A(20 - x_A) = x_A(10 - y_A)$

$20y_A - x_Ay_A = 10x_A - x_Ay_A$. The cross terms cancel here (they will not always), leaving $20y_A = 10x_A$.

$$y_A = \tfrac12 x_A$$

d Describe the curve geometrically, and state the general rule this illustrates.

It is the straight line from $O_A = (0,0)$ to $O_B = (20,10)$ — the diagonal of the box.

General rule: when both people have the same Cobb–Douglas weights, the contract curve is always the diagonal, $y_A = \frac{Y}{X}x_A$. Identical tastes means efficiency requires identical ratios $y_i/x_i$, and the only way two identical ratios can add up to $Y/X$ is if both equal $Y/X$.

2

A full equilibrium solve. Same preferences as problem 1 ($u_i = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$ for both), but now with endowments: $\omega_A = (10, 0)$ and $\omega_B = (0, 20)$. A owns all the $x$; B owns all the $y$.

a Normalize prices and write each person's income as a function of $p$.

Set $p_y = 1$, $p_x = p$. Then $m_A = 10p + 0 = 10p$ and $m_B = 0 + 20 = 20$.

b Write each person's demand for good $x$.

Half of income on each good.

$x_A = \dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{10p}{p} = 5$  (constant — A owns only $x$, so price and income effects exactly offset).

$x_B = \dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{20}{p} = \dfrac{10}{p}$.

c Clear the market for $x$ and solve for $p^*$.

$5 + \dfrac{10}{p} = 10 \Rightarrow \dfrac{10}{p} = 5 \Rightarrow \boxed{p^* = 2}$.

Sensible: $x$ is the scarcer good (10 units versus 20), so it trades at a premium.

d Find the full equilibrium allocation.

$x_A = 5$ and $y_A = \frac12 m_A = \frac12(10\cdot 2) = 10$. $x_B = 10/2 = 5$ and $y_B = \frac12(20) = 10$.

$$p^* = 2,\qquad A = (5,10),\qquad B=(5,10)$$

e Run all three checks: the other market, both budgets, and whether the allocation is efficient.

• $y$ market: $10 + 10 = 20 = Y$ ✓

• A's budget: spends $2(5) + 10 = 20$, income $2(10) = 20$ ✓. B's: $2(5)+10 = 20 = $ income ✓

• Efficient? Identical tastes, so problem 1's rule applies: the contract curve is the diagonal $y_A = \frac{Y}{X}x_A = 2x_A$ (note this box has different totals than problem 1's). At $x_A = 5$: $y_A = 10$ ✓. Exactly as the First Welfare Theorem promises.

• Gains: $u_A$ went from $\sqrt{10\cdot 0} = 0$ to $\sqrt{50} \approx 7.07$; same for B. Starting with none of one good makes Cobb–Douglas utility zero, so trade is worth an enormous amount here.

3

Walras' Law as a tool. In some two-good exchange economy with $p_y = 1$, the excess demand for $x$ has been computed for you:

$$z_x(p) = \frac{8}{p} - 4$$

a State Walras' Law for this economy.

$p\,z_x(p) + z_y(p) = 0$ for every $p > 0$ — the value of aggregate excess demand is zero at all prices, because everyone's budget balances.

b Find $z_y(p)$ without knowing anything about preferences.

$z_y = -p\,z_x = -p\left(\dfrac{8}{p} - 4\right) = -8 + 4p = 4p - 8$.

c Find $p^*$ from each market separately and confirm they agree.

From $x$: $\frac8p - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow p^* = 2$. From $y$: $4p - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow p^* = 2$. Same answer — which is the content of Walras' Law, not a coincidence.

d At $p = 1$, describe the disequilibrium in words and say which way the price must move.

$z_x(1) = 8 - 4 = +4$: excess demand for $x$. $z_y(1) = 4 - 8 = -4$: excess supply of $y$. (Check: $1(4) + (-4) = 0$ ✓)

Too many people want $x$ at that price, so $p$ must rise toward 2. Notice the two imbalances are always mirror images — with two goods, excess demand for one is excess supply of the other.

4

Build an offer curve. $u_A = x_A^{1/3}y_A^{2/3}$ with endowment $\omega_A = (9,3)$. Normalize $p_y = 1$.

a Write A's income as a function of $p$, then her demands $x_A(p)$ and $y_A(p)$.

$m_A(p) = 9p + 3$. With weight $1/3$ on $x$:

$x_A(p) = \frac13\cdot\frac{9p+3}{p} = 3 + \dfrac1p$,    $y_A(p) = \frac23(9p+3) = 6p + 2$.

b Eliminate $p$ to get the offer curve as a relationship between $x_A$ and $y_A$.

Solve the easier equation for $p$ first.

From $y_A = 6p+2$: $p = \dfrac{y_A - 2}{6}$, so $\dfrac1p = \dfrac{6}{y_A-2}$ and

$$x_A = 3 + \frac{6}{y_A - 2}, \qquad y_A > 2$$

As $p \to \infty$, A holds almost no $x$ ($x_A \to 3$) and a lot of $y$; as $p \to 0$, $x$ is nearly free and $x_A \to \infty$.

c Find A's autarky price — the $p$ at which she chooses not to trade at all.

Set $x_A(p) = 9$: $3 + \frac1p = 9 \Rightarrow \frac1p = 6 \Rightarrow p = \frac16$. Confirm with the other good: $y_A = 6(\frac16)+2 = 3$ ✓ — exactly the endowment.

d Verify that this price equals A's MRS at her endowment, and explain why it must.

$\mathrm{MRS}_A(\omega) = \frac{1/3}{2/3}\cdot\frac{3}{9} = \frac12\cdot\frac13 = \frac16$ ✓

Why: "choosing not to trade" means the endowment is the optimum, and an interior optimum requires tangency, $\mathrm{MRS} = p$. So the autarky price is the MRS at the endowment. This is why the equilibrium price ratio always lies between the two people's autarky prices — outside that interval, both want to be buyers or both want to be sellers, and no trade can clear.

5

Diagnose an allocation. A $10\times 10$ box, both people with $u = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$. Someone proposes the allocation $A = (2,6)$.

a What does B receive, and what is each person's MRS there?

$B = (10-2,\ 10-6) = (8,4)$.

$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \dfrac{y_A}{x_A} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3$ and $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac12$.

b Is the allocation Pareto optimal? Justify in one sentence.

No: $3 \neq \frac12$, so the indifference curves cross rather than touch and a lens of mutually improving trades remains open.

c Which direction should the goods flow, and what range of exchange rates would both accept?

A has the higher MRS for $x$, so $x$ should flow to A and $y$ to B. Any exchange rate $t$ with $\frac12 < t < 3$ units of $y$ per unit of $x$ makes both strictly better off.

d Give one concrete improving trade and verify both utilities rise. Then state where on the contract curve this economy could end up.

Trade one unit of $x$ from B to A for one unit of $y$ from A to B (rate $t = 1$, safely inside the range):

A: $(2,6) \to (3,5)$, $u_A: \sqrt{12} = 3.46 \to \sqrt{15} = 3.87$ ✓

B: $(8,4) \to (7,5)$, $u_B: \sqrt{32} = 5.66 \to \sqrt{35} = 5.92$ ✓

Identical Cobb–Douglas tastes $\Rightarrow$ contract curve is the diagonal $y_A = x_A$. Trading stops somewhere on that diagonal; exactly where depends on bargaining power, or on prices if this is a competitive market.

6

Perfect substitutes. $u_A = 3x_A + y_A$, $u_B = x_B + 3y_B$, $X = Y = 12$, and $\omega_A = \omega_B = (6,6)$.

a Compute both MRSs. What is unusual about them?

$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{3}{1} = 3$ and $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{1}{3}$. Both are constants — they do not depend on the bundle, because the indifference curves are straight lines. They are never equal, so the tangency condition can never hold in the interior.

b Describe the set of Pareto optimal allocations.

If A always values $x$ more, where does the shipping of $x$ toward A stop?

Since $\mathrm{MRS}_A > \mathrm{MRS}_B$ everywhere, any interior allocation can be improved by moving $x$ toward A and $y$ toward B. It stops only at a boundary: either A holds all the $x$ ($x_A = 12$) or B holds all the $y$ ($y_A = 0$).

Pareto set $= \{x_A = 12\} \cup \{y_A = 0\}$ — the right edge together with the bottom edge of the box.

c For which price ratios does A want to buy only $x$ and B only $y$?

A buys only $x$ when the price is below her valuation: $p < 3$. B buys only $y$ when $x$ is expensive relative to his valuation: $p > \frac13$.

So both hold when $\frac13 < p < 3$ — and if $p$ ever equalled $3$ or $\frac13$, that person would be indifferent across their whole budget line.

d Find the competitive equilibrium.

Guess a $p$ in the window from (c). A spends her whole income $m_A = 6p + 6$ on $x$, so $x_A = \frac{6p+6}{p}$. Clearing requires A to absorb all 12 units:

$\dfrac{6p+6}{p} = 12 \Rightarrow 6p + 6 = 12p \Rightarrow p^* = 1$, which does lie in $(\frac13, 3)$ ✓

$$p^* = 1,\qquad A = (12,0),\qquad B = (0,12)$$

Check B: income $6(1)+6 = 12$, all spent on $y$, so $y_B = 12$ ✓. Utilities: $u_A: 24 \to 36$ and $u_B: 24 \to 36$.

e Is the equilibrium on the Pareto set from (b)? What does that tell you about the First Welfare Theorem at corners?

$A = (12,0)$ sits at the intersection of both edges, so yes — it is Pareto optimal.

The First Welfare Theorem holds here even though $\mathrm{MRS}_A \neq \mathrm{MRS}_B$. The theorem was never really about tangency; tangency is just what efficiency looks like in the smooth interior case. The theorem only needs local non-satiation, which linear preferences certainly satisfy.

7

Second Welfare Theorem, start to finish. $u_A = 6\ln x_A + y_A$ and $u_B = 3\ln x_B + y_B$, with $X = 9$, $Y = 12$, $\omega_A = (5,5)$, $\omega_B = (4,7)$. A planner wants to implement the allocation $A = (6,8)$, $B = (3,4)$.

a First, confirm the target is Pareto optimal by finding the contract curve.

$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \frac{6}{x_A}$, $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac{3}{x_B} = \frac{3}{9 - x_A}$. Setting them equal:

$6(9 - x_A) = 3x_A \Rightarrow 54 = 9x_A \Rightarrow x_A = 6$.

The contract curve is the vertical line $x_A = 6$ (quasilinear, as expected), and the target has $x_A = 6$ ✓. Also note the target is feasible: $6+3 = 9$ and $8+4 = 12$ ✓

b Find the price ratio that would support it.

The supporting price is the common MRS at the target: $p^* = \frac{6}{6} = 1$. Cross-check with B: $\frac{3}{3} = 1$ ✓

c Compute the lump-sum transfer required, and state exactly who pays whom.

At $p^*=1$, the target bundle costs A: $1(6) + 8 = 14$. A's endowment is worth $1(5)+5 = 10$.

A is short by $14 - 10 = 4$. So B transfers 4 units of income (say 4 units of $y$) to A before trading begins: $\omega'_A = (5,9)$, $\omega'_B = (4,3)$.

d Verify that the market, left alone with the new endowments, actually delivers the target.

New incomes at $p=1$: $m_A = 5 + 9 = 14$, $m_B = 4 + 3 = 7$.

A: $\mathrm{MRS} = p \Rightarrow \frac{6}{x_A} = 1 \Rightarrow x_A = 6$; then $y_A = 14 - 6 = 8$ ✓

B: $\frac{3}{x_B} = 1 \Rightarrow x_B = 3$; then $y_B = 7 - 3 = 4$ ✓

Markets clear: $6+3 = 9$ and $8+4 = 12$ ✓. Note that the quantity of $x$ each person consumes did not depend on the transfer at all — that is the quasilinear structure: transfers move $y$ around and leave the efficient $x$-split untouched.

8

Find the flaw. Back to the running example: $u_A = x^{3/4}y^{1/4}$, $\omega_A = (4,8)$; $u_B = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$, $\omega_B = (8,4)$; $X = Y = 12$. A classmate claims:

"At $p = 1$, the allocation $A = (7,5)$, $B = (5,7)$ is a competitive equilibrium. Both bundles cost exactly what each person's endowment is worth, and the markets clear, so we are done."

a Check the two claims your classmate actually verified. Are they right about those?

Feasible? $7 + 5 = 12$ and $5+7 = 12$ ✓

Affordable? A spends $1(7)+5 = 12$, and her endowment is worth $1(4)+8 = 12$ ✓. Same for B. So yes — both claims are correct.

b Now test the condition they skipped. Is A optimizing at that bundle?

$\mathrm{MRS}_A = 3\cdot\frac{y_A}{x_A} = 3\cdot\frac57 = \frac{15}{7} \approx 2.14$, but $p = 1$.

Since $\mathrm{MRS}_A > p$, A values an extra unit of $x$ at more than it costs her. She is not at an optimum — she would keep buying $x$. (B fails too: $\mathrm{MRS}_B = \frac13\cdot\frac75 = \frac{7}{15} \approx 0.47 < 1$, so B would sell more $x$.)

c What would A actually choose at $p=1$, and what is the correct equilibrium?

At $p=1$, $m_A = 12$ and the share rule gives $x_A = \frac34(12) = 9$, $y_A = 3$. So A chooses $(9,3)$, not $(7,5)$ — and that is the equilibrium, since B symmetrically chooses $(3,9)$ and both markets clear.

Interesting wrinkle: the claimed price $p=1$ was right; only the allocation was wrong.

d State the general lesson in one sentence, and say whether $(7,5)$ is at least Pareto optimal.

Lesson: budget-feasible plus market-clearing is not enough — equilibrium requires each bundle to be the best affordable bundle, not merely an affordable one.

Efficient? No. On the contract curve $y_A = \frac{3x_A}{27-2x_A}$, $x_A = 7$ would require $y_A = \frac{21}{13} \approx 1.6$, not 5. The MRSs differ ($2.14$ versus $0.47$), so a lens is still open and gains from trade remain on the table.

9

When the price refuses to be unique. $u_A = \min(x_A,y_A)$ and $u_B = \min(x_B,y_B)$, $X = Y = 12$, $\omega_A = (4,8)$, $\omega_B = (8,4)$.

a Write each person's demand functions at price $p$ (with $p_y=1$).

With perfect complements the consumer always sets $x = y$, then spends the whole budget.

Set $x_i = y_i$ in the budget: $p x_i + x_i = m_i \Rightarrow x_i = y_i = \dfrac{m_i}{p+1}$, with $m_A = 4p+8$ and $m_B = 8p+4$.

b Compute total demand for $x$ and show what happens when you try to solve for $p^*$.

$x_A + x_B = \dfrac{(4p+8)+(8p+4)}{p+1} = \dfrac{12p+12}{p+1} = \dfrac{12(p+1)}{p+1} = 12$.

Total demand equals 12 identically — the market-clearing equation becomes $12 = 12$, which is true for every $p$ and therefore determines nothing. There is a continuum of equilibria, one for each positive price ratio.

c Find the equilibrium allocations at $p = 1$ and at $p = 3$, and say who prefers which.

$p=1$: $x_A = \frac{12}{2} = 6$, so $A = (6,6)$ and $B = (6,6)$. Both get utility 6.

$p=3$: $x_A = \frac{20}{4} = 5$, so $A = (5,5)$ and $B = (7,7)$, utilities 5 and 7.

B prefers the higher $p$: B is the one holding more $x$, so a higher price for $x$ makes him richer. A prefers the lower price. Every one of these is a legitimate competitive equilibrium.

d Why did the tangency method fail here — and does the First Welfare Theorem still hold?

Why tangency failed: L-shaped indifference curves have a kink at the corner, and the MRS is undefined there, so "$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$" is not an available equation. Uniqueness of equilibrium needs strictly convex preferences; perfect complements are convex but not strictly so.

First Welfare Theorem: still holds, with no trouble at all. Every one of these equilibrium allocations has $x_i = y_i$ for both people, which puts it on the diagonal — the contract curve. The theorem needs local non-satiation, not differentiability.

★

Which tool do I reach for?

1. Does the question mention prices?
No → it is an efficiency question. Go to step 2.    Yes → it is an equilibrium question. Go to step 3.

2. Efficiency route. Identify the preference type first. Smooth and interior $\Rightarrow$ set $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$ after substituting $x_B = X - x_A$, $y_B = Y - y_A$. Kinked or linear $\Rightarrow$ argue directly (diagonal, or edges).

3. Equilibrium route. Normalize $p_y=1$ → incomes $= p\omega_x + \omega_y$ → demands as functions of $p$ → clear one market → substitute back → check the other market.

4. Asked to support a given allocation? That is the Second Welfare Theorem: the price is the common MRS at the target; the transfer is (cost of target) $-$ (value of endowment).

5. Asked whether an equilibrium is efficient? First Welfare Theorem — yes, automatically, and you can show it by noting both MRSs equal the same $p$.

★

Definitions in one line each

TermOne line
Endowment $\omega$What each person owns before trade; the starting point in the box and the source of all income.
Feasible allocationThe two people's holdings add up to the totals $X$ and $Y$ — a point inside the box.
Pareto improvementA move that helps someone and hurts nobody.
Pareto optimalNo Pareto improvement is available; interior version: $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$.
Contract curveThe set of all Pareto optimal allocations, drawn in the box.
CoreThe efficient allocations that also beat the endowment for both people — efficient and voluntary.
Offer curveOne person's chosen bundle as $p$ sweeps from 0 to $\infty$; always passes through $\omega$.
Autarky priceThe $p$ at which a person chooses not to trade; equals their MRS at $\omega$.
Excess demand $z_x(p)$$x_A(p) + x_B(p) - X$; equilibrium is where it hits zero.
Walras' Law$p\,z_x + z_y = 0$ at every price; clear one market and the other clears free.
Competitive equilibriumA price ratio plus an allocation such that everyone is optimizing and all markets clear.
★

The formulas

Efficiency condition (interior)

$$\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$$

Substitute $x_B = X - x_A$ and $y_B = Y - y_A$ before solving.

Cobb–Douglas MRS

$$\mathrm{MRS} = \frac{\alpha}{\beta}\cdot\frac{y}{x}$$

For $u = x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}$ — any exponents, summing to 1 or not ($x^2y \Rightarrow \frac{2y}{x}$). The workhorse of this unit.

General CD contract curve

$$y_A = \frac{r_B Y x_A}{r_A X - (r_A-r_B)x_A}$$

$r_A = \frac{\alpha_A}{\beta_A}$, $r_B = \frac{\alpha_B}{\beta_B}$ (the exponent ratios). If $r_A = r_B$: the diagonal $y_A = \frac{Y}{X}x_A$.

Budget constraint

$$p\,x_i + y_i = p\,\omega_{ix} + \omega_{iy}$$

Income is endowment value. The line always passes through $\omega$ and pivots there.

Cobb–Douglas demand here

$$x_i = \frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_i+\beta_i}\cdot\frac{p\omega_{ix}+\omega_{iy}}{p}$$

Share rule with endowment income substituted in. Do not use a fixed $m$.

Walras' Law

$$p\,z_x(p) + z_y(p) = 0$$

$z_x(p) = x_A(p)+x_B(p)-X$ is excess demand for $x$ (same for $z_y$; negative = excess supply). Holds at every price — solve one market, use the other as a check.

Equilibrium condition

$$x_A(p^*) + x_B(p^*) = X$$

One equation, one unknown. Then substitute back for the allocation.

Supporting price (2nd WT)

$$p^* = \mathrm{MRS}_A(z^*) = \mathrm{MRS}_B(z^*)$$

Transfer $= p^*x^*_A + y^*_A - (p^*\omega_{Ax}+\omega_{Ay})$.

★

The four preference worlds, compressed

TypeContract curveEquilibrium quirk
Cobb–DouglasSmooth arc, corner to cornerUnique, interior, tangency works
Perfect complementsThe diagonalMRS undefined at kinks; $p^*$ can be a whole range
Perfect substitutesTwo edges (an L)Corner allocations; compare constant MRS to $p$
QuasilinearA vertical lineEfficiency fixes $x$ only; transfers move $y$ alone
★

Traps, ranked by how often they cost marks

1. Treating income as fixed. $m$ moves with $p$ here, always. If your demand function has a plain number where $p\omega_x + \omega_y$ belongs, stop and fix it.

2. Forgetting to convert B's variables. $\mathrm{MRS}_B$ must be written in $x_A$ and $y_A$ before you can set it equal to $\mathrm{MRS}_A$.

3. Calling efficient "fair." A corner where one person has everything is Pareto optimal. Efficiency and equity are separate axes.

4. Confusing affordable with optimal. Equilibrium needs the best affordable bundle for each person, not merely a feasible one (practice problem 8).

5. Redrawing the contract curve after a transfer. Redistribution moves the budget line, never the contract curve — the curve depends only on preferences and totals.

6. Applying tangency to kinks or straight lines. Identify the preference type in the first ten seconds and pick the matching method.

7. Solving both markets. Wasted time and a chance to make an arithmetic error. Walras' Law means one is enough — the second is your check.

8. Reporting only the price. "An equilibrium" means $p^*$ and all four quantities. Write them out.

The five sentences worth memorizing verbatim

1. In general equilibrium, income is the value of your endowment, so the budget line pivots around $\omega$.

2. Efficiency means no lens: $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$, and the set of all such points is the contract curve.

3. Walras' Law: the value of aggregate excess demand is zero at every price, so with two goods one market clearing implies the other.

4. First Welfare Theorem: both people face the same $p$, so both MRSs equal $p$, so they equal each other — every competitive equilibrium is Pareto optimal.

5. Second Welfare Theorem: with convex preferences, any efficient allocation can be reached by a lump-sum redistribution followed by free trade at the supporting prices.

What comes next. The production economy takes the same machinery — tangency, prices, welfare theorems — and replaces "what already exists" with "what a firm chooses to make." The contract curve becomes the production possibilities frontier, and $\mathrm{MRS} = \mathrm{MRT}$ takes over from $\mathrm{MRS}_A = \mathrm{MRS}_B$.
